bugs: No correctness bugs found. Minor: `=A1 (2)` lexes `A1` as a function name (#NAME?) rather than #PARSE!, and a ref immediately followed by whitespace+'(' is silently treated as a call.
Formulas that fail to parse are never rewritten by structural edits or copy (documented), so fixing a typo later leaves stale references — a usability trap rather than a spec violation.
Dependents() hands out live internal sets ('must not be mutated'); safe today because recalc never touches the index, but a fragile contract.
strengths: Fully iterative pipeline (shunting-yard, stack VM with jumps for IF/IFERROR, iterative Kahn+Tarjan) with no recursion-limit games.
Dyadic 2-D range index gives O(log²) point lookups independent of how many ranges exist; incremental structural edits that relocate compiled code and only recalc formulas that actually lost cells.
Randomised differential test checks every shortcut (incremental recalc, relocation, change lists) against a freshly built sheet; perf tests pin the spec's timing scenarios.
NOTES.md is exhaustive on design and every open behavioural decision, with measured timings.
weaknesses: Dense, highly optimised code: GC-tracking tricks (1-tuples, atomic instruction tuples), many `# type: ignore`, awkward aliased imports, tagged-tuple AST/work-stack in `generate` — steeper onboarding.
Two parallel paths for structural edits (text rewrite + compiled-code relocation) must stay in sync; mitigated by the differential test but adds coupling.
ArgumentTypeError inheriting from both TypeError and ValueError is unusual API surface.

bugs: Recursive-descent parser and recursive AST evaluation rely on `sys.setrecursionlimit(20000)` set/restored around every set/copy/structural call; process-global mutation, and nesting beyond the limit silently degrades to #PARSE!/#VALUE! via caught RecursionError.
Structural edits rebuild the whole sheet (`self.__init__()` then re-store everything) and recalculate every cell: O(sheet) per insert/delete.

RangeIndex: any range spanning more than 256 tiles (e.g. a single-column range taller than ~16k rows) goes to an untiled list scanned on every lookup, so thousands of tall column SUMs slow down edits anywhere on the sheet; within a tile every rect is scanned too.
Negative zero is not normalised (`=-0*1` returns -0.0; ROUND(-0.4,0) gives -0.0) — cosmetic.
`_check_axis` does no type check: `insert_rows(1.5)` produces float cell keys and corrupts the store.
Off-grid references in formulas evaluate to #NAME? and a range with an off-grid endpoint is #PARSE! (documented decision, but surprising given #REF! exists).
Sheet exposes extra non-API public methods `value` and `iter_rect`.
strengths: Clean, idiomatic, compact code (NamedTuples, match statements, Node.rect protocol makes single-ref-as-range handling elegant).
Tokenizer never raises, so even unparseable formulas get their references rewritten; rewrite keeps unchanged tokens byte-for-byte.
Large black-box test suite written from the brief plus a decisions suite pinning every documented choice; cycle, structural and copy cases well covered.
Honest NOTES.md with an explicit 'Known limits' section.
weaknesses: Scalability is the weakest of the three: full recalc on structural edits, recursion-dependent parsing/evaluation, and a range index that degrades to linear scans.
Evaluates every reachable dependent on each edit with no short-circuit when inputs are unchanged.
tools/bench.py is a one-liner script with poor style; no randomised/differential testing.

bugs: `copy` and `_parse_range` call `.replace('$', '')` before validating the type, so a non-str src/dst raises AttributeError instead of ValueError.

`copy` iterates every position of the source rectangle (not just populated cells) and seeds recalc with every key, so copying a large sparse block such as a whole column does ~1M iterations, stores and index lookups.
Deleting past the grid edge (`delete_rows(1048576, 2)`) is accepted silently; the other two submissions reject it.
Lenient re-tokenisation for rewriting skips an unterminated quote and then treats the rest as tokens, so `="abc & A1` gets its `A1` rewritten although it is inside a (broken) string literal.
strengths: No recursion anywhere: shunting-yard parser, explicit-stack compiler, flat VM with conditional jumps, iterative Tarjan.
Per-axis multi-resolution range index with bucket-level containment checks; tested explicitly against thousands of tall single-column ranges.

Incremental structural edits: only formulas whose tracked refs/ranges are affected are rewritten and recompiled, with a clear invariant ('any change in target shows up in the text') plus dependents-of-removed-cells seeding; endpoint-wise rewriting preserves whitespace around ':'.
Good module docstrings and a NOTES.md that explains both design and decisions.
weaknesses: Adding a function requires touching two modules (ARITY in _formula, FUNCTIONS in _evaluator, plus _AGGREGATES) — easy to get out of sync.
String-opcode VM dispatch via if/elif chain is readable but slower than table dispatch.
Test suite is thinner than X/Y: no differential/randomised testing, fewer parametrised cases, and one structural test searches a hard-coded list of candidate cells to find the moved formula.
Structural edits still rebuild the whole dependency index (O(cells)) even when only a few formulas change.

result.rationale: X is the most engineered of the three: fully iterative parsing and evaluation, a logarithmic range index, incremental structural edits that avoid re-tokenising, and a randomised differential test that actually guards those shortcuts; its cost is denser, more optimisation-laden code. Z shares the sound architecture (no recursion, multi-resolution range index, incremental structural edits with a clear invariant) and is easier to read, but has a few rough edges in argument validation, a copy that iterates the whole rectangle, and a lighter test suite. Y is the cleanest to read and has a thorough black-box test suite, but its design choices — recursive evaluation propped up by a global recursion-limit hack, whole-sheet rebuild and recalc on every structural edit, and a tile index that degrades to linear scans for tall ranges — make it the least scalable and least robust. All three document their decisions well; X's NOTES.md is the most complete.
